Civic literacy · 2026 general electionNovember 3, 2026 · checked as of

A new architecture of American leadership

Not left versus right. Top versus bottom.

In November 2026, voters propelled an unprecedented cohort of barrier-breaking leaders into statehouses, the Senate, Congress, and City Halls. This interactive intelligence grid transforms election outcomes into an accessible civic education tool.

The 2026 midterms swept Democrats into power in states Trump carried easily, including Kansas, Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Ohio. The winners ran as pastors, loggers, pediatricians and teachers against corruption, billionaire money, the price of gas and groceries, and Big Tech’s data centers. This is the who, the why and the how, with the evidence and the places where the story is less tidy than it sounds.

01 · The scale

Counts are preliminary. Alaska and Mississippi Senate races were uncalled on November 6.

02 · Who moved

The coalition, group by group

Compared with Trump’s 2024 vote, Republican House candidates lost ground with nearly every group. The biggest swings came from Hispanic voters, independents and the young. The smallest came from white voters without a college degree, the core of the Republican base, which matters for how far “even conservatives” really goes.

Republican share of the vote by group. Source: Brookings, Nov. 6, 2026.

03 · Why

Six forces beneath the wave

None of these is a culture-war issue. Each is about money, power or basic needs: what things cost, who gets rich from government, who controls the platforms and the power grid, whether you can see a doctor, and whether anyone checks the people at the top.

04 · How

The winning playbook

Across very different states and ideologies, the winners repeated a handful of moves. Read these as patterns in the coverage, not a proven formula.

    Municipal power matrix

    Who actually runs your city

    Most of the roughly 11,000 U.S. municipalities with 2,500 or more residents use one of two structures. Which one your city uses decides whether the mayor you elect runs anything, and who answers when a service fails.

    Compare the two structures

    Forms of government

    Share of 10,969 municipalities with 2,500+ residents, ICMA 2018.

    Claims about efficiency

    The often-repeated line that council-manager cities are “nearly 10% more efficient” comes from a 2011 IBM benchmarking study of 100 large cities, not peer-reviewed research. ICMA reports that 66% of Moody’s Aaa-rated cities had a professional manager in 2016. Both are associations: well-off, stable cities may simply be more likely to choose professional management.

    $61,723

    Average pay for a full-time mayor (ICMA 2018).

    $9,286

    Average pay for a part-time mayor. Low pay narrows who can afford to serve.

    27.2%

    Share of city council seats held by women (ICMA 2018). 32% of cities elect some or all of their council by district.

    Mayors of the 100 largest cities

    Ballotpedia, November 2026. At the start of 2026, 81% of the top-100 population lived under a Democratic mayor; 22 of these seats were on the 2026 ballot.

    What the 2026 mayoral results show

    Term limits drove much of the turnover. In Chandler, Irving, Knox County and Boca Raton the incumbent could not run, so the seat changed hands without any voter rejecting a sitting mayor. A change in a mayor’s party is not always a change in voters’ minds.

    Many mayoral races are officially nonpartisan. Party labels do not appear on the ballot in Chandler, Irving or Los Angeles, so descriptions such as “Democratic gain” rely on candidates’ registrations or endorsements, which are not always public.

    Defeating an incumbent is rare. Los Angeles was the exception: Karen Bass became the first sitting mayor there to lose since 2005, after the Palisades Fire and rising homelessness. Most incumbents on this list who ran were re-elected comfortably.

    The calendar is local. Florida cities often vote in March, Wisconsin in April, Texas in May and North Dakota in June. A common mistake is to assume every result came from November 3: this year’s mayoral races above were decided in March, April, June and August as well.

      The shadow government

      Nearly 40,000 special districts

      A special district is a separate local government created for one job: fire protection, water, sewers, libraries, hospitals, mosquito control. Many can levy property taxes and issue bonds, and each has its own board. The Census Bureau counted 39,555 in 2022, and 40,199 in its 2025 update, out of roughly 91,000 local governments. The commonly quoted “38,000” is the 2017 count.

      The tax stack over one home

      Illustrative rates

      One address can sit inside a county, a city, a school district and several special districts, each taxing separately. The rates here are hypothetical and chosen only to show the structure; look up your own on your county assessor’s tax bill.

      Annual tax

      Taxing boards

      Elected seats

      Ask yourself: how many of these boards’ members could you name? How many of their elections did you vote in?

      What special districts do

      Census Bureau function counts, 2022, grouped by this site. Total 39,555.

      Case study · Missoula County, Montana · February 2026

      On February 10, county commissioners declared 12 special-district boards elected by acclamation because every candidate was unopposed, among them the Missoula Irrigation District. They cancelled elections in 15 more, including the Missoula Rural Fire District and the Turah Meadows Sewer and Water District, because nobody filed at all; those seats were opened for appointment. Local coverage shows the same thing happened in 2018, 2021, 2022 and 2025. It is routine, which is the point.

      Missoula County release →

      When only landowners vote

      Some water districts limit voting to landowners, weighted by acreage. The Supreme Court upheld this in Salyer Land Co. v. Tulare Lake Basin (1973) and Ball v. James (1981), reasoning that these districts serve land rather than people. It is one of the few places in American government where one person, one vote does not apply.

        Campaign capital

        Follow the money

        The 2026 midterms are projected to be the most expensive on record, and a small number of very large donors supplied much of the outside money. This is the money side of the “top versus bottom” story: how much was spent, who paid, what the biggest races show, and how to check the money where you live. Every figure has a date and a source. Where outlets disagree, we show the range.

        How much

        $11.9B

        Projected total federal election spending in 2026, up from $8.9 billion in 2022 (about $10.2 billion adjusted for inflation). OpenSecrets projection, reported Nov. 4, 2026.

        $3.9B

        Projected spending by outside groups, up 85% from four years earlier. OpenSecrets projection.

        $1.47B+

        “Dark money,” gifts from donors who are not named, flowing to outside groups. A lower bound and a record; 2024’s total was $1.35 billion. OpenSecrets.

        515

        donors who each gave at least $1 million supplied more than 70% of all super PAC money so far: $4.2 billion. Public Citizen, Oct. 27, 2026.

        ~$2B

        from just the 20 biggest donors to federal races, through the mid-October filing deadline. New York Times ranking, reported Nov. 1, 2026.

        $737M

        in corporate political spending through Oct. 23, up 60% from the 2024 presidential cycle and more than four times 2022. Public Citizen.

        How we got here

        Since the 2010 Citizens United ruling, the biggest donors have moved to the center

        On January 21, 2010, the Supreme Court’s Citizens United v. FEC decision removed restrictions on independent spending by corporations and unions. Outside spending, which candidates do not control, has grown from $574 million in 2008 to close to $4.5 billion in 2024, and most of it is spent by super PACs.

        Outside spending in presidential-election cycles, in millions of dollars. OpenSecrets, published Jan. 24, 2025. The 2012 and 2024 figures are reported as “nearly $1.3 billion” and “close to $4.5 billion.”

        1.5% → 14–16%

        The top 100 individual donors’ share of all federal election spending: 1.5% in 2008 ($80.9 million of $5.3 billion), and between 14% and 16% since 2016. OpenSecrets, Jan. 24, 2025.

        $2.6B

        spent in 2024 by billionaire donors and their families, nearly 20% of all federal election spending, over 80% of it through channels not allowed before 2010. It has multiplied by a factor of 163 since the ruling. Roosevelt Institute report, Oct. 2025, citing Americans for Tax Fairness.

        $290M+

        from one billionaire to outside spending groups in 2024, about the combined gifts of 3 million small donors. OpenSecrets data, as cited in the Roosevelt Institute fact sheet.

        Dark money has grown the same way. Nonprofits that do not name their donors spent $1.2 million on federal elections in 2006 and $257 million in 2012 (OpenSecrets data, via Common Cause, Jan. 2015). The Brennan Center counted more than $1.9 billion across the 2024 federal races, up from about $1 billion in 2020, and at least $4.3 billion since 2010. It says that is probably a substantial undercount. The 2006 to 2012 numbers and the 2020 and 2024 numbers measure different things.

        Most Americans see the problem. In Pew Research Center surveys from mid-2023, 80% said big campaign donors have too much influence on what members of Congress do, 70% said people in their own district have too little influence, and 72% supported limits on how much individuals and organizations can spend on campaigns. Brennan Center polling from June 2, 2026, cited in its October article, found that nine in ten voters say government prioritizing billionaires and large corporations is corrupt, and that majorities in both parties blame campaign donations.

        Researchers disagree about what the ruling did. An NBER working paper (July 2023, not peer-reviewed) compared the 23 states that had banned independent political spending with states that had not. After the ruling it found total income about 2% higher and labor income up to 3% higher in the states that had had bans, more turnover among governors and legislators in both parties, less polarized legislatures, and fewer state enforcement actions against labor and consumer-protection violations. The authors read this as more political competition. The Roosevelt Institute fact sheet cites other state-level studies of the same kind of states (we did not read them) that found corporate tax rates cut by 4 to 8 percent and Republican candidates’ success rates up 4 to 11 percentage points. Both are studies of state governments.

        Which industries

        Corporate money

        Corporate political spending reported to the FEC through Oct. 23, 2026, in millions of dollars (Public Citizen).

        Cryptocurrency, online betting and Big Tech and AI together gave $391.3 million, 53% of corporate spending. Public Citizen says the real total is probably higher, because not all corporate money is reported.

        What the biggest races show

        Texas Senate

        $573.2M

        in ad spending in the general election, the most of any non-presidential race in U.S. history (AdImpact, reported Nov. 3, 2026).

        • Outside groups from both parties spent over $205 million on the general election through September, and more than 98% of it supported Republican Ken Paxton (Texas Tribune, Oct. 1).
        • Texas PAC, the group connected to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, spent $131 million. President Trump’s super PAC added nearly $24 million.
        • Democrat James Talarico spent $61 million on ads in the general election (AdImpact).
        • In the primaries, of $49.4 million spent supporting Cornyn, Paxton and Talarico, 36% came from groups that do not disclose donors, and the $13.2 million of dark money backing Cornyn was more than his own campaign raised (Brennan Center, May 2026 roundup, published June 9).

        Result: Talarico won, 55% to 43%, with about 99% of precincts reporting.

        Michigan Senate Democratic primary

        $30.6M

        spent by AIPAC’s United Democracy Project to support Haley Stevens and oppose Abdul El-Sayed, the most it has ever spent on a single race (Sludge, Aug. 3, 2026).

        • In all, more than $60 million went to support Stevens or oppose El-Sayed, against about $3.5 million of outside spending for El-Sayed (Al Jazeera, Aug. 2). About $6.5 million of the $60 million comes from a group that had not reported to the FEC, so that part is from local media.
        • AIPAC’s PAC and super PAC have spent more than $104 million this cycle, the second cycle in a row above $100 million (Sludge).

        Result: El-Sayed won the primary, 49% to 47%, and then the general election.

        Three governors’ races

        Money figures: Brennan Center, “Who’s Trying to Buy the Governor’s Mansion?”, Oct. 27, 2026, drawing on news reports and campaign filings that it did not independently verify. Results are from this site’s checked notes.

        Georgia

        Republican Rick Jackson self-funded over $100 million and outspent Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms “five to one.” Result: Bottoms won, 54.2% to 45.8% with 95% counted.

        Ohio

        Republican Vivek Ramaswamy loaned his campaign at least $36 million, and Jeff Yass gave at least $30 million to a super PAC backing him. He and allied groups spent over $120 million on ads, more than triple the spending for Democrat Amy Acton. Result: Acton won, 52.3% to 44.4% with 97.7% counted.

        Wisconsin

        Three megadonors (Diane Hendricks and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein) accounted for 92% of Republican Tom Tiffany’s fundraising in the three months before the report. State law limits labor union PACs to $86,000 for Democrat David Crowley. Result: Crowley won, about 54% to 45%, and Tiffany conceded.

        In Texas, Michigan, Georgia and Ohio, the side that spent more lost. Four races do not prove that money never wins. They show that it does not always win. Before the election, The Washington Post reported that Republicans’ roughly half-billion dollars of spending since the summer did not appear to have moved the polls, as the Brennan Center notes.

        The rules changed, and the referee is missing

        More money is moving through fewer limits, with little enforcement

        • Independent expenditures by super PACs and other groups hit a record $2 billion through the end of September, up 51% from the last midterm cycle after inflation.
        • In June the Supreme Court struck down limits on how much party committees can spend in coordination with their candidates (National Republican Senatorial Committee v. FEC). The Senate GOP spent $48 million in coordination with its candidates through August, the bulk of the $63 million spent this way by all four congressional party committees. The NRSC’s spending alone is three times what all four committees spent in coordination by the end of August 2022.
        • Party-affiliated super PACs have increased their spending tenfold since 2014. Together they spent $494 million through September, including $280 million from two Senate Republican-linked groups, SLF PAC and Texas PAC.
        • The Federal Election Commission has lacked a quorum for most of this cycle. With only two of its six seats filled, it cannot investigate, impose penalties or make new rules.

        Brennan Center, Ian Vandewalker, “Big Money Breaks Records, Boosts GOP,” Oct. 13, 2026. Independent expenditures run through September; coordinated spending through August.

        The other side of the ledger

        Small donors are giving, in huge numbers

        $586M

        raised from small-dollar donors for Democratic candidates, causes and organizations in the second quarter of 2026. The average gift was $39. ActBlue, July 9, 2026.

        15M

        contributions in that one quarter, including 573,000 from first-time donors. It was ActBlue’s best non-presidential quarter on record.

        Compare the scale: it took 15 million small gifts in one quarter to raise $586 million, while 515 donors gave $4.2 billion to super PACs over the cycle so far. These are different measures. ActBlue is one platform, on the Democratic side, for one quarter, and the figure comes from its own release. The super PAC number covers the whole cycle so far.

        What people are doing about it

        Voters in three states moved to limit big money

        On November 3, 2026, Montana voters approved Initiative 194, “the Montana Plan,” with about 65% of the vote (Daily Montanan, Nov. 4). It would bar corporations, nonprofits and other organizations from spending money to support or oppose candidates, parties or ballot measures. Individuals acting on their own and political committees are exempt (NBC Montana, Nov. 6).

        It is not settled. It takes effect on January 1, 2027 unless a court blocks it. A federal lawsuit filed on election night by the Frontier Institute, the Montana Republican State Central Committee and other groups argues it violates their First Amendment rights and asks a court to pause it.

        Michigan. Voters approved Proposal 2 on November 3 with about 81% yes, 3,550,297 to 805,646 with most precincts counted (ClickOnDetroit, Nov. 4). It bars regulated utilities such as DTE Energy and Consumers Energy, and government contractors with more than $250,000 in state contracts, along with people associated with them, from making campaign contributions (WXYZ). The Mackinac Center for Public Policy sued in federal court on November 3, arguing the measure violates the First Amendment because it would require journalists, nonprofits and others to file reports when they speak about elected officials.

        Alaska. In the August 18 primary, voters approved a measure reinstating limits on individual campaign contributions, by roughly 3 to 1 in early results (Alaska Public Media) and by more than 70% according to the Brennan Center. It sets $2,000 per candidate per two-year cycle for individuals and $4,000 for political groups, adjusted for inflation once a decade, and takes effect after the November general election. Alaska has had no individual limit since a federal appeals court struck down its $500-a-year limit in 2021.

        Other reforms on the table. The Brennan Center’s policy agenda (Jan. 20, 2026) proposes four changes to campaign money: amend the Constitution to restore campaign finance limits, ban big donations from government contractors, require groups that spend on federal campaigns to disclose their major donors, and publicly fund campaigns. New York already matches small contributions to state candidates at up to $12 to $1. Legislators or voters in 23 states have passed resolutions calling for a constitutional amendment on campaign finance. These are proposals from a think tank, not law.

        Closer to home

        A real example: San Diego City Council, 2022

        Local officials control zoning, building permits, public contracts and labor agreements, so the people affected by those decisions have reasons to fund local campaigns. There is no national database of municipal campaign money, so the honest unit of analysis is one city at a time.

        MapLight / Common Cause California analysis of 2,678 individual donors.

        796 donors who gave the legal maximum, 30% of all donors, supplied about 67% of individual contributions. Real estate and construction interests gave about 17% of council campaign funding. Concentration, not a single industry, is the clearest pattern.

        How to check your own money

        1. For federal races, search donors and committees on FEC.gov, the official record.
        2. For your city or state, find your city clerk’s, county elections office’s or secretary of state’s campaign finance portal.
        3. Download contributions for the races you care about as a spreadsheet.
        4. Sort by employer and occupation. Developers, contractors, and lobbying firms are usually visible.
        5. Look for independent-expenditure committees, which can spend unlimited amounts if they do not coordinate with the candidate.
        6. Compare the money with the votes those officials later cast.
        Where the numbers disagree, and what we could not confirm
        • Elon Musk’s total. Reports range from $366 million (New York Times, via the Brennan Center, Oct. 13) to $445 million (Public Citizen, Oct. 27), $446 million (Al Jazeera, Oct. 27) and $483 million for Musk and his company (Brennan Center, Oct. 29, data through Oct. 14). The difference is the cutoff date and what is counted.
        • Texas Senate. $432 million is all spending in the primaries and general election through September (Texas Tribune). $573.2 million is ad spending alone in the general election (AdImpact). They measure different things.
        • Dark money has two counts. OpenSecrets’ $1.47 billion (so far in 2026) and $1.35 billion (2024) count gifts to outside spending groups. The Brennan Center’s $1.9 billion for 2024 also counts direct spending and TV and online ads, so it is a wider measure, and the Brennan Center calls it an undercount.
        • Totals still moving. OpenSecrets’ $11.9 billion is a projection until all reports are filed. Dark money and corporate totals will rise as late reports come in.
        • Donor lists differ a little. Al Jazeera and Public Citizen both use FEC data but count differently. For example, they give the Uihlein family $150 million and $146 million.
        • Not found. A single total for billionaires’ giving, and the share of 2026 money from donors giving under $200. We could not read opensecrets.org directly, so OpenSecrets figures are quoted from IBTimes (Nov. 4).

          Law & courts

          The justice ecosystem

          Most people meet the justice system locally: a sheriff’s deputy, a prosecutor, a judge, a county jail. In much of the country, voters choose the people who lead those offices, often in races with only one name on the ballot. This page shows who holds which power, the numbers behind it, what happened at the polls in 2026, and what you can look up and ask where you live. Every figure has a date and a source.

          The shape of it

          Nearly 2 million people are confined, in more than 6,000 places

          ~2M

          people confined in prisons, jails, immigration detention, juvenile facilities and other places. Prison Policy Initiative, Mar. 11, 2026.

          $445B

          a year, at least, is the cost of the whole system.

          465,000

          people are held before trial, 426,000 of them in local jails. About 120,000 more are in jail after a conviction, generally for misdemeanors with sentences under a year.

          +58%

          growth in ICE detention between 2025 and 2026, about 25,200 more people. The report says immigration detention accounts for virtually all of the growth in mass incarceration since its last report.

          $54.3B

          spent on federal immigration policing and detention in 2025, up from $20 billion in 2017. That is 13% of government criminal legal system spending.

          12% · 15%

          Local jails hold about 12% fewer people, and state prisons about 15% fewer, than in 2019.

          Number of facilities by type, 2026 (Prison Policy Initiative). The report also counts military prisons, civil commitment centers, psychiatric facilities and prisons in the territories.

          What to take from this. Local jails are the most numerous kind of facility, 3,116 of them, and most sheriffs’ offices run one. The fastest growth is in immigration detention, which is federal. That is why who runs your county jail, and what agreements they sign, matters.

          Gets the job: typically elected, county by county.

          The numbers: 2,900 sheriffs’ offices were 20% of general-purpose police agencies but employed 25% of their sworn officers; about 10% of sheriffs’ sworn officers were assigned to jail duties (BJS, Dec. 31, 2020).

          Prosecutor (district attorney)

          Gets the job: elected in 45 states.

          Decides: whether to charge, what to charge, plea offers, bail requests and diversion programs.

          The numbers: only 23% of 3,231 prosecutor elections from 2020 to 2024 were contested (UNC, May 13, 2026).

          Judge

          Gets the job: some form of election in 39 states; appointed in others.

          Decides: bail, trials, sentences and what the law means.

          The numbers: trial judges are chosen in nonpartisan elections in 21 states and partisan elections in 11 (Brennan Center, updated Apr. 2023).

          Public defender

          Gets the job: funded and organized by counties or states, or contracted out.

          Decides: defends people who cannot afford a lawyer.

          The numbers: Pennsylvania was one of only two states that did not fund public defense for decades (Spotlight PA, Apr. 1, 2026).

          County sheriff

          Elected

          • — Covers the whole county
          • — Usually runs the county jail
          • — Patrols unincorporated areas
          • — Serves warrants and court orders
          • — Answers to voters

          City police chief

          Appointed

          • — Covers one city
          • — Usually no long-term jail
          • — Enforces state and city law
          • — Hired by the mayor or manager
          • — Can be removed by them

          Prosecutors

          The most powerful office most people never choose between candidates for

          Local prosecutor elections were held in 45 states from 2020 to 2024. Of 3,231 regular elections, 23% were contested. Voters had less choice than in any period the researchers have studied.

          Share of local prosecutor elections that were contested. Prosecutors and Politics Project, Carolina Law, May 13, 2026.

          In 2026, all 15 of Oregon’s district attorney races have one candidate. Bolts found it is the only cycle this century in which that is true. Five of the 12 incumbents first got the job by a governor’s appointment, not an election. Lawyers and advocates told Bolts that harsh campaigns, fear of career damage and low pay keep challengers out.

          Trials are rare

          Most cases end in a plea

          2% · 90%

          of about 80,000 federal defendants in fiscal 2018, about 2% went to trial and about 90% pleaded guilty. About 8% had their cases dismissed (Pew Research Center, 2019).

          State data are patchier. In 2017, jury trials were fewer than 3% of criminal cases in the 22 jurisdictions with data, including 0.86% in Texas and 2.91% in New York (National Center for State Courts, via Pew). Critics argue that defendants who go to trial and lose can face much higher sentences than those who plead. That claim comes from a 2018 defense lawyers’ report, not from Pew’s data.

          What to take from this. If trials are rare, most outcomes are set earlier, by what a prosecutor charges and what plea they offer. That is why a contested prosecutor race is often the only moment voters can weigh in on those choices.

          Sheriffs, jails and immigration

          Many sheriffs now act as immigration enforcement partners

          1,412

          active 287(g) agreements between ICE and local agencies as of Feb. 13, 2026, across 40 states and territories. NPR, Feb. 17, 2026.

          1,130+

          agreements signed in 2025 alone, compared with just 45 signed in 2019, during President Trump’s first term (NPR).

          234 of 254

          Texas counties, by a bill author’s count, are covered by a state law that requires counties running a jail to join the program. It takes effect Jan. 1, 2026, with compliance required by Dec. 1, 2026 (WJLA, July 2025).

          A 287(g) agreement lets local officers do some immigration enforcement. There are three models. Under the jail model, everyone booked into a local jail is checked for legal status. Under the warrant model, local officers serve administrative warrants on people already in the jail. Under the task force model, officers can stop, question and arrest people for immigration violations, with ICE supervisor approval. ICE reimburses participating agencies for the salary and benefits of each trained officer, and for overtime up to 25% of salary.

          States differ. Florida’s governor has effectively required local agencies to sign. Virginia’s governor ordered state agency agreements ended. Critics, including a University of California, Irvine law professor, warn of racial profiling and costly lawsuits, and the Government Accountability Office has said the program needs better oversight. The Department of Homeland Security calls the profiling allegations “categorically false,” and a Heritage Foundation analyst calls the concerns overblown.

          What to take from this. A sheriff’s choice about 287(g) is made locally, and in some states it is required by law. Whether your county has an agreement, under which model, is a public fact you can ask about.

          Sheriffs: money and accountability

          Elected sheriffs answer to voters, and have to raise money to win

          • Who pays for sheriff campaigns. A Common Cause report with Communities for Sheriff Accountability (December 2021) examined campaign finance records of sheriffs in 11 states, covering less than 3% of sheriffs’ offices. It counted about 13,000 apparent conflicts of interest, mostly between 2010 and 2021. It treated gifts from jail-related businesses, and from companies that might do business with a sheriff’s office, such as construction, food service and health care, as potential conflicts. About $6 million, roughly 40% of the $15.7 million it examined, fell in that category. In Bristol County, Massachusetts, the jail’s health care contractor spent more than $20,365 on Massachusetts sheriffs’ campaigns, $12,040 of it for the county’s sheriff, and the state’s sheriffs paid it $9.82 million in contracts from 2012 to 2021. The authors did not judge whether any gift was illegal, chose sheriffs by a mix of public interest and random selection, and are advocacy groups.
          • Election years change behavior. A study of 57 California counties from 2003 to 2020 (Su and Buerger, American Journal of Political Science, 2024) found traffic-fine revenue fell 30% in sheriff election years, and only in the election year. The drop was larger when the incumbent ran again or the race was highly contested. The authors expected sheriffs to ease enforcement to avoid voter anger, and did not test that motive directly. It is one state.
          • Sheriffs who answer only to voters. A 2025 Georgetown Law Journal article by Vanderbilt law professor Farhang Heydari describes “constitutional sheriffs” as sheriffs who view themselves as the highest authority in their county, answerable only to their electorate. They have declared opposition to gun control measures, pandemic restrictions and environmental protections, among other things. He notes that other sheriffs have declared opposition to immigration and abortion restrictions, so it is not one-sided. He argues that courts should again decide when a sheriff’s refusal to enforce a law amounts to neglect of duty, as state courts once did.
          • A county that wrote a removal rule. In November 2022, Los Angeles County voters approved Measure A, a charter amendment that lets the Board of Supervisors remove a sheriff by a four-fifths vote. The grounds include violating a law related to the sheriff’s duties, flagrant or repeated neglect of duty, misusing public funds, falsifying an official document, and obstructing an investigation. The sheriff gets written notice and a chance to be heard first. The county’s Sheriff Civilian Oversight Commission had urged the Board to put it on the ballot.

          What to take from this. Between elections, a sheriff may face few formal checks. Researchers are measuring how elections shape what sheriffs do, and one large county has written a rule for removing one. Campaign finance reports for a sheriff’s race are usually public, though the Common Cause researchers said getting records from some sheriffs’ offices was hard.

          Before trial

          Jails and bail

          Most people in a local jail on a given day have not been convicted. Since 1997, all of the net growth in jails has come from people held before trial (Prison Policy Initiative).

          One state’s experiment. Illinois became the first state to end cash bail on September 18, 2023. In the first year, Loyola University researchers found jail populations fell, but far less than predicted. The share of people who missed court dates went from about 17% to about 15%. They found no documented rise in crime comparing the first six months of 2023 with the first six months of 2024, and said plainly: “We can’t say whether it’s had an impact on crime.” The findings were preliminary.

          What to take from this. A few years of data from one state can tell you what did not happen. It cannot settle what caused it, and honest researchers say so.

          The right to a lawyer

          The promise is national. The funding is local.

          In 1963 the Supreme Court held that a poor person’s trial cannot be fair unless a lawyer is provided. Estimates say between one-third and one-half of people who qualify are represented by assigned or contract lawyers, according to the Vera Institute (Feb. 17, 2026), which says public defense has been funded at “drastically lower levels” than prosecution and police for decades.

          A close look at Pennsylvania. Counties are still the main funders. The state began giving $7.5 million a year in 2023, spread across 67 counties. A committee found the state about 400 lawyers short for adult criminal cases, and nearly 40% of lawyers hired in the past five years have left. In up to 20% of cases, court records showed no representation or “unknown” representation, though the data may be incomplete. The ACLU of Pennsylvania sued in 2024, and the case is ongoing (Spotlight PA, Apr. 1, 2026).

          Courts

          How states choose supreme court justices

          Initial selection method, all 50 states (Ballotpedia). Kansas voters rejected a switch to elections on August 4, 2026.

          Assisted appointment (often called the Missouri Plan): a commission screens candidates, the governor picks one, and the judge later faces a yes-or-no retention vote.

          Retention elections are a later step, not a separate method, so a chart that counts them as a method alongside elections double-counts states.

          2026 results

          State supreme court elections

          • Texas. Democratic challengers defeated all four Republican justices seeking reelection to the Texas Supreme Court, including the Chief Justice. Republicans still hold a 5–4 majority. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals now has a 6–3 Republican majority.
          • Ohio. Democrats gained a seat on the Ohio Supreme Court. Republicans keep a 5–2 majority.
          • North Carolina. Justice Anita Earls won reelection. Republicans keep a 5–2 majority. The race drew over $8 million, on track to be the most expensive state supreme court election of the year.
          • Montana. Amy Eddy won. A citizens’ initiative to put nonpartisan judicial elections into the state constitution passed with 68%.

          Brennan Center State Court Report, Nov. 4, 2026 (updated Nov. 5). The authors say the results are not likely to immediately change any state high court majorities, and set up fights for majorities in 2028. Money is a factor in these races: Wisconsin’s 2025 Supreme Court race drew about $57 million in outside spending (Brennan Center, as cited by the Roosevelt Institute).

          The cost of the bench

          State supreme court races are the most expensive ever

          $157.3M

          spent on state supreme court races in the 2023–24 cycle by candidates, interest groups and parties. That is 35% more than 2019–20 and almost twice 2015–16, adjusted for inflation. Brennan Center, Feb. 26, 2026.

          $85M · $70M

          Interest groups spent $85 million (54%) and candidates $70 million (45%). It was the first time outside groups outspent the candidates.

          30%

          of the 119,000 TV ads in these races mentioned abortion rights, up from 3% in 2020. Courts also decide voting rules and district maps, which drew major donors.

          The biggest races: Wisconsin’s 2023 race at $51 million, then the most expensive judicial election in U.S. history; Pennsylvania at $27 million; North Carolina at $10.5 million, a state record; and two Montana races at $6.8 million and $5.9 million.

          The money came from both sides. Groups on the left supplied 64% of interest-group spending: groups backing liberal candidates spent $55 million and conservative-backed groups $30 million. The report names dark money groups on both sides, among them A Better Wisconsin Together and WMC in Wisconsin. Fair Courts America disclosed that $9 million of its $12 million came from Richard Uihlein, while some groups reveal donors only in tax filings long after the election.

          What to take from this. When a court decides abortion, voting rules or district maps, who sits on it becomes worth spending on. Voters in states that elect judges are the ones who see that money in their ads.

          Police and accountability

          What the data say, and what the law allows

          1,314

          people killed by police in 2025, down 5% from 1,383 in 2024. It is the first decrease in six years. Mapping Police Violence, Feb. 2026.

          3.6

          people a day, on average. The group warns that federal agencies are expanding use of force and some states are rolling back reforms such as limits on vehicle pursuits.

          Qualified immunity. On March 23, 2026, in Zorn v. Linton, the Supreme Court held that a Vermont sergeant who used a wristlock on a protester at a sit-in was protected from a lawsuit, because no earlier case with similar facts clearly said his conduct was unconstitutional. Courts, the decision says, generally need to point to such a case. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, dissented.

          Mapping Police Violence counts publicized killings from news reports and official sources. Other outlets cite slightly lower 2025 totals.

          Safety

          What is happening to crime

          −51%

          Homicides in 30 large cities in the first half of 2026 were 51% below the 2022 peak, 18% below the first half of 2025 and 31% below the first half of 2019.

          ~4.0

          per 100,000: the 2025 national homicide rate, an estimate that would be the lowest since at least 1900 if FBI data confirm it.

          Carjacking fell 47% in the first half of 2026, the largest drop of 13 offenses. Drug offenses rose 12%, the largest rise. The Council on Criminal Justice says there is “no single or easy explanation,” that the report is not evidence for or against any policy, and that the cities studied may not represent the nation (July 23, 2026).

          Who is affected, and who can vote

          The justice system also decides who gets a voice

          ~4M

          Americans were denied the right to vote because of a felony conviction in the 2024 federal election. The Sentencing Project, Oct. 29, 2026.

          1 in 22

          voting-age Black Americans is blocked from the ballot, more than three times the rate of non-Black Americans.

          56%+

          of Virginia voters approved an amendment on Nov. 3, 2026 that restores voting rights automatically when people leave prison. Before, they had to petition the governor.

          Maine, Vermont and Washington, D.C. let citizens vote while incarcerated. In 2026, Missouri restored voting rights to more than 41,000 people on felony probation and parole, and a federal court ruling sharply narrowed Virginia’s policy. The Virginia count is early reporting, not the certified result.

          Who is imprisoned. The Sentencing Project’s 2021 report, using 2019 federal data, found Black Americans were imprisoned at nearly five times the rate of white Americans, and one in 81 Black adults was in state prison. That report is old, so treat the exact ratio as an estimate. The direction is the point.

          The jail voting gap

          About 78% of people held in U.S. jails in 2024 had not been convicted of the charge they were held on (Prison Policy Initiative, using federal data). Most pretrial detainees keep the right to vote, and the sheriff running their jail, the prosecutor and sometimes the judge may all be on their ballot.

          There is no national figure for how many actually vote. A court-ordered Massachusetts report released in June 2026 found 1% turnout among eligible people in jail in the 2024 primary and 5% in the general election. Harris County, Texas opened the state’s first jail polling place in November 2021.

          “Unconvicted” and “eligible” are not the same: some detainees are ineligible for other reasons.

          Jail voting that worked

          When a jail runs a polling place, people vote

          25%

          of people held in Cook County Jail (Chicago) voted in the June 2022 primary: 1,384 of 5,560. That beat the 20% turnout of registered voters in the city, and about half of them used same-day registration. Prison Policy Initiative, Oct. 25, 2022.

          <7%

          In the same jail’s 2018 primary, before in-person voting, only 394 people voted, by absentee ballot. In the 2020 general election, more than 2,000 of about 5,400 did, roughly 37%.

          13

          of an estimated 26 eligible people voted at the Harris County Jail in Texas in the March 2022 primary. In the first election there, in November 2021, 96 did.

          Why it is hard. The average jail stay is about 28 days, too short for a mail ballot to go out and come back. Jail is not a recognized reason for an absentee ballot in several states. Many people do not know they can vote or think their charge disqualifies them. Photo ID can be confiscated at intake, as in Texas, and registration forms and stamps can be hard to get. Cook County officials estimate 80% of people in their jail are eligible to vote (Center for Public Integrity, Sept. 15, 2022).

          Where it exists. Jail polling places have run in Cook and Will counties in Illinois, Washington, D.C., Denver, Harris County in Texas and Los Angeles County (Prison Policy Initiative, 2022).

          The law. In 1969, in McDonald v. Board of Election Commissioners, the Supreme Court framed a jailed voter’s claim as a right to receive absentee ballots and noted nothing in the record showed they were absolutely barred from voting. In 1974, in O’Brien v. Skinner, it struck down a New York law that let some jailed people vote absentee but not people held in their home county, calling the exclusion “wholly arbitrary” for people awaiting trial or serving misdemeanor sentences who had no other way to vote.

          What to take from this. Most people held before trial keep the right to vote. Whether they can use it depends on whether the jail and the county elections office make it possible, and both are run locally.

          What voters decided in 2026

          A record of the year, so far

          • August 4, Kansas: voters rejected a switch to electing supreme court justices.
          • November 3, Virginia: voters approved automatic voting rights restoration after prison, with more than 56% in early reporting.
          • November 3, Montana: 68% voted to put nonpartisan judicial elections in the constitution.
          • November 3, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina: the supreme court races above, with Democrats gaining seats in Texas and Ohio and Republican majorities holding.
          • All year, Oregon: all 15 district attorney races had one candidate.

          We found no national tally of 2026 district attorney or sheriff results, so this list covers what we could confirm.

          Look it up, then ask

          Build your own picture of your county

          Look up

          • Who is on your ballot, from sheriff to judge: Ballotpedia’s sample ballot lookup.
          • How often your state’s prosecutor races are contested: the Prosecutors and Politics Project.
          • How many people your county jails and sends to prison, over time: Vera’s Incarceration Trends.
          • Your state’s numbers and profile: Prison Policy Initiative state profiles.

          Ask candidates

          A sheriff

          Does your office have a 287(g) agreement, and under which model? How many people in your jail are held before trial, and for how long? Who investigates when someone dies in custody?

          A district attorney

          Will you publish data on charges, plea offers, dismissals and diversion? How do you decide when to ask for bail?

          A judge or judicial candidate

          How do you weigh pretrial release? Who funds your campaign?

          Where the numbers disagree, and what we could not confirm
          • Police killings. Mapping Police Violence counts 1,314 for 2025. Other outlets cite about 1,200. The difference is how and when deaths are counted.
          • Racial disparity. The Sentencing Project’s five-to-one figure is from 2019 data and a 2021 report. A Prison Policy Initiative page appears to give a higher ratio, about six to one; we saw that only in a search summary and did not read it.
          • Illinois bail. The Loyola findings are from the first year and are preliminary. Later reports by advocacy groups and think tanks reach different conclusions, and we did not read them in full.
          • 287(g) agreements. The count rose through 2026. NPR’s 1,412 is as of Feb. 13. Later counts we saw in search results came from sources we did not read.
          • Judges. The count of states that elect judges is from a 2023 update. We did not find 2026 results for Michigan or Washington supreme court races, or Wisconsin’s April 2026 race.
          • Sheriff campaign money. The Common Cause report is by advocacy groups, covers a small share of sheriffs’ offices, defines “conflict” broadly, and did not test whether any gift was illegal or changed any decision.
          • Election-year traffic fines. One state, California, from 2003 to 2020. The motive is the authors’ expectation, not a tested result.
          • Jail voting. Turnout figures are county and advocate counts. There is no national figure. We read McDonald only as the later O’Brien opinion quotes it. For Los Angeles County’s Measure A we confirmed that it led by a wide margin on election night, but did not open a source with the final percentage.
          • Not found. A national tally of 2026 district attorney and sheriff elections, the number of people in state prisons from the 2026 report we read, and a national count of public defender shortages. A researcher told Stateline the national picture is “a complete black box.”
          Sources for this section

            Interactive electoral mechanics

            Ranked choice, round by round

            In ranked choice voting (also called instant runoff), you rank candidates. If no one has more than half of first choices, the last-place candidate is eliminated and those ballots move to each voter’s next choice still in the race. That repeats until someone has a majority of the ballots still counting. Washington, D.C. used it for the first time in June 2026.

            2026 at the ballot box

            • 16 jurisdictions used it in 2026, including Alaska, Maine, NYC and San Francisco.
            • Longmont, CO adopted it with about 56%.
            • Irvine, CA measure leading, not yet called.
            • Honolulu rejected it: 44.6% yes among votes cast on the question.
            • Alaska repeal losing on election night with about 52% no; absentee ballots count for 15 days.

            1. Shape the electorate

            Each bloc is a group of voters who cast the same ranking. Drag a slider to change a bloc’s size, or change its rankings. Leave a choice blank to model voters who rank fewer candidates. Total:

            Candidates are fictional. Ties for last place are broken by ballot order; real jurisdictions use lot or other statutory rules.

                  Languages

                  How translation works

                  This site is written in English, and English is the original. When you choose Español or العربية, your browser translates the page on your device where it can. Chrome and Edge on desktop do this from the language buttons. Firefox, Safari and phone browsers have their own Translate feature, which the language buttons explain.

                  The site sends no text anywhere to be translated. Translations can contain errors, so the English original is the authoritative version. Names, quotations and legal designations are left as written, and charts are not translated.
